name: Smile maxxing
lead: Smile maxxing is a looksmaxxing-community term for optimising how one's smile looks, whether through teeth (whitening, alignment, cosmetic dentistry), the gums and lips, or the way the smile is expressed. People use it because the smile is one of the most visible features of the face in conversation and photos, and changes to tooth colour, shape, spacing or facial expression can alter how friendly, confident or attractive a person appears.

The term has no formal definition and no published research uses it. Related topics have encyclopedic coverage: the muscles and types of smile, the perception of smiling people, and cosmetic dental procedures [1][2][3].

Dental routes range from over-the-counter whitening to veneers and orthodontics [2][5]. Expressive routes focus on whether the smile engages the eyes (a Duchenne smile) and how much of the teeth and gums show [1][4].

paras: A smile is produced mainly by muscles at the corners of the mouth. A Duchenne smile also engages the muscle around the eye (orbicularis oculi), and research summarised in encyclopedias associates it with positive emotion and with being judged as more sincere [1][4]. A voluntary smile that uses only the zygomaticus major is sometimes called a Pan Am smile [1].

Smiling is reported to make a person seem more likable, approachable and, in some summaries, more trustworthy, although perception varies by culture [1][4]. Smiles were rare in Western portraiture before the nineteenth century [4].

Wikipedia notes that the Duchenne smile is named for French neurologist Guillaume Duchenne, who identified two distinct smile types in the mid-19th century, and that a non-Duchenne smile involves only the zygomatic major [6]. Research by Messinger, Fogel and Dickson reported in 2001 that Duchenne smiling is uniquely associated with positive emotion [6]. Cross-cultural work has found that smiling is more common in the US and France than in China or Japan, and that in some cultures a smiling person may be seen as less intelligent [6]. The earliest known photograph of a smile is attributed to William Mansel, around 1853 [6]. Cheek dimples are described as an inherited trait linked to a bifid zygomaticus major [6]. Wikipedia also notes that chronic Botox use around the eyes can prevent a Duchenne smile [6].

Dental work often associated with smile optimisation includes whitening, bonding, veneers, enamel contouring, orthodontics and gum contouring [2][3][5]. Wikipedia describes whitening as the most common cosmetic dental procedure, and describes bonding with tooth-coloured composite, thin porcelain veneers that usually require some tooth reduction, gum lifts that reshape tissue or underlying bone, and straightening with braces or clear aligners [2]. Cosmetic dentistry is not recognised as a specialty by the American Dental Association, which recognises prosthodontics and orthodontics as the specialties most focused on aesthetics [2].

For tooth whitening, in-office treatment may lighten teeth by two to seven shades and home products usually by one or two, with some rebound after intensive sessions. Tooth sensitivity is the most common side effect [5]. In the EU, retail whitening products may contain up to 0.1 percent hydrogen peroxide and professional use up to 6 percent, while the US FDA endorses gels under 6 percent hydrogen peroxide or up to 16 percent carbamide peroxide [5]. Reshaping of enamel is permanent because removed enamel cannot be replaced [2].

Aesthetic dentistry is traced to Newell Sill Jenkins (1840-1919), an American dentist working in Dresden who developed a porcelain enamel, and the American Society for Dental Aesthetics was conceived in 1976 and the American Academy of Cosmetic Dentistry founded in 1984 [2]. Tray-based bleaching was introduced in the late 1960s and supported in published research in 1989, and whitening strips arrived in the late 1980s [5]. Smiles were rare in Western portraiture before the nineteenth century, and Victorian and Edwardian photographs seldom showed them, which Wikipedia attributes to convention [6][4]. Looksmaxxing communities adopted the 'maxxing' suffix for optimising a feature, and smile maxxing applies it to the mouth and expression.

US spending on whitening reached about 15 billion dollars by 2010, and in 2010 the UK General Dental Council raised patient-safety concerns about whitening by untrained staff [5]. Wikipedia's article on cosmetic dentistry notes ethical concerns about dentists calling themselves cosmetic dentists regardless of training and questions about whether general dentists should handle complex smile makeovers [2]. In expression, researchers cited by Wikipedia report that smiling makes a person seem more likable and approachable, with perception varying by culture [6].

card.summary: Forum shorthand for optimising your smile, from teeth to expression; a loose umbrella with no formal protocol.
card.note: An umbrella term; risks depend on whether it means dental procedures or expression practice.

quick.overview:
Smile maxxing is a looksmaxxing term for improving how your smile looks. It can mean dental changes such as whitening or alignment, or practising how the smile is expressed.

There is no formal definition or research using the term; it overlaps with cosmetic dentistry and smile training.
quick.mechanism: Dentally, it involves procedures that change tooth colour, shape and position. Expressively, it concerns which facial muscles are used, for example whether a smile engages the eyes (Duchenne smile).
quick.risks: Risks depend on the method. Dental procedures such as veneers can involve irreversible tooth reduction, while expression practice carries little reported risk. No studies of the term itself were found.

chain: Improve tooth colour, alignment or gum display, and practise a natural expression
Teeth look brighter and more even; the smile reads as more genuine
The face looks friendlier and more approachable in conversation and photos
angle.text: Smile maxxing groups together dental work and expression practice aimed at a better-looking smile. Dental changes alter how the teeth look, and expression practice changes how a smile reads in the face.
